messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mark is a 34-year-old school counselor who has been struggling with profound psychological distress following an incident where he accidentally caused serious injury to another individual. This traumatic event continues to haunt him, and his symptoms have become increasingly debilitating over time. The accident occurred at a local community sports event when Mark was coaching a youth baseball team. In the heat of the moment, he made a decision that led to one of the players being severely injured. The intense stress and shock from this incident has left deep psychological scars. Since then, any form of medical procedures or related smells trigger vivid memories of the accident. These triggers are particularly potent because they bring back the overwhelming fear and guilt associated with the event. Mark's coping mechanisms have become maladaptive over time as he tries to manage these triggers. He constantly keeps his mind occupied with work-related tasks and other activities, which serves both as a distraction from intrusive thoughts and memories and as a way to avoid thinking about what happened. This mental preoccupation helps him navigate through the day but has started to take a toll on his relationships and job performance. For instance, during a recent medical check-up at the hospital, the sterile smell of antiseptic immediately transported Mark back to the emergency room where he had seen the injured player. He experienced intense physical reactions—sweating, rapid heartbeat, and nausea—and struggled to stay focused. The memory felt so real that it was as if the event were happening again in the present moment. The intensity of these memories has left him with a sense of self-doubt. Mark is certain that he cannot trust himself to make the right decisions anymore. This belief compounds his fear and anxiety, making it even more difficult for him to cope with daily life. He feels as though his life has been irrevocably destroyed by this trauma, and these negative appraisals exacerbate his feelings of guilt and self-blame. His negative appraisals have influenced his maladaptive strategies. The constant need for mental distraction arises from a deep-seated belief that he cannot handle the memories and emotions tied to the accident. By keeping himself busy with work or other activities, Mark hopes to avoid the intense emotional pain and fear associated with the event. This cycle of thoughts and behaviors has created a self-reinforcing loop where his triggers lead to vivid, full-sensory reliving of the memory. These memories then fuel his negative appraisals and physical reactions, which in turn increase his reliance on maladaptive strategies like mental distraction. The result is an overwhelming sense of vigilance and fear, especially at night when he has difficulty falling asleep because he feels a need to stay alert. As Mark’s symptoms have intensified over time, the impact on his daily life has become more pronounced. His wife reports that he has been distant and irritable, and this strain in their relationship is evident. At work, Mark finds it increasingly challenging to focus on counseling students effectively due to his constant mental preoccupation with thoughts of the accident. What finally brought Mark to seek help was a recent episode where he experienced a severe panic attack during a school event. He realized that if he did not address these issues, they would continue to erode his quality of life and relationships further. He is most afraid of never being able to trust himself again or fully escape the memories and guilt associated with the accident. Mark hopes for relief from the constant distress and a way to rebuild his confidence and ability to function effectively in his role as a school counselor and in his personal life. He recognizes that professional help might be the key to breaking this cycle of avoidance, negative appraisals, and intense emotional reactivity.
